title: Client service and complaints for a service business
audience: Owners and staff of service businesses that take bookings, visit clients at home or on site, or work from a fixed premises, and who deal with the client before, during and after the job.
referencesAtStart: No regulator page is cited in this lesson. Source: the customer-service workbook uploaded for this lesson, reworded.
learningOutcomes: Confirm a booking, its scope, its exclusions and what the client must provide, before the work starts.
Set expectations about the result, the time window and pre-existing defects, and record what was agreed.
Handle a complaint in a fixed order: listen, acknowledge, check the record, offer options within your authority, record the outcome and follow up.

instruction.heading: Service starts at the first contact
instruction.body: For a service business, the client's experience begins with the first enquiry, not with the first visit. Answer enquiries promptly, and say clearly what you can do, when you can do it and what it will cost. Confirm every booking in writing, with the date, the time window, the address or site, the scope, the package and the list of included and excluded items. Ask open questions about what the client wants to achieve and what problem they are trying to solve. Then ask what the job needs from the client: access to water and power, parking, a gate code, the location of any pets, and any building or strata rules that apply on the day. Most client dissatisfaction comes from expectations that were never stated. A client who knows what is excluded is less likely to be surprised at handover. Keep the language plain, and avoid promising a result you have not yet inspected.

instruction.heading: Setting expectations and recording them
instruction.body: Expectations need to be agreed before work begins. Explain what a good result looks like for this job and what it cannot achieve. For example, an odour that comes from damp under a floor may not be removed fully by surface cleaning, and an old mark on a wall may stay visible after treatment. Tell the client if the time on site will be longer than expected, and tell them early rather than at the end of the visit. Link this conversation to the condition record taken before work, so that you and the client can point to the same pre-existing defects. Where the client asks for something outside the agreed scope, give a clear price and a clear time before doing it, and confirm the change in writing. At handover, walk the client through the finished areas, point out any limits, and ask them to confirm they are satisfied with the result they can see. Keep a short handover note with the date, the time the job finished and any open point.

instruction.heading: Handling a complaint in a fixed order
instruction.body: A complaint is a useful signal, and it is also a chance to keep the client. Start by listening without interrupting or correcting the client, even if you think they are mistaken. Acknowledge the inconvenience and the effort the client has taken to raise it, and say you want to sort it out. An apology for the experience is appropriate even before the cause is known, but do not admit fault you have not checked. Next, check the facts against the job record, the condition photos where they were taken, and the booking confirmation. Do not blame the client, the product or another worker. If you do not know the answer, say so and give a time when you will come back with it. Offer options that you have the authority to deliver, such as returning to correct the work, removing a residue at no extra charge, or a partial credit where the work cannot be corrected. Record the complaint with the date, the client's contact details, the detail given, the action agreed and the outcome. Then follow up after the fix, confirm that the client is satisfied, and close the record. If the matter involves injury, damage to property or a claim against the insurance policy, stop negotiating and pass it to the person you have named for escalation.

procedure: Confirm every booking in writing, including the included items, excluded items and what the client must provide on site.
On arrival, greet the client, confirm the scope and check the access, water and power arrangements.
Record the condition of the property or item, and any exceptions the client has agreed to, before work begins.
At handover, walk the client through the finished work, point out any limits, and note the agreed follow-up.
When a complaint arrives, listen, acknowledge the concern and say when you will respond.
Check the complaint against the job record, offer options within your authority, and record the complaint, the action and the outcome.
Follow up after the fix, confirm the client is satisfied, and close the record with the date.

workedExamples.situation: EXAMPLE, invented for teaching: a client is told at home that a visit is complete. They say a product used on a kitchen bench top has left a residue, and they ask for the full fee back. The job record has photos of the bench top taken before work, and the booking confirmation lists that product as an included item.
workedExamples.decisionPrompt: What do you do first, and what do you offer?
workedExamples.reasoning: Listen to the full complaint without arguing. Acknowledge that the result is not what the client expected, and apologise for the experience. Check the pre-work photos against the bench top as it is now, and inspect it with the client on site. If the residue comes from the product, offer to remove it at no extra charge, and set a time to return. If it cannot be removed, offer a partial credit within your authority, and say that anything beyond that goes to the person you have named for escalation. Record the complaint, the action and the agreed follow-up date, and check with the client after the fix.

equipmentAndPpe: Booking log or job card, with the included and excluded items listed.
Pre-work photo log or condition checklist, with the client's permission to photograph.
Complaint register, which can be a simple form or a spreadsheet.
No specific personal protective equipment is needed for the conversation itself.

commonErrors.error: Promising a result before the job has been inspected.
commonErrors.prevention: Inspect first, then say what can and cannot be achieved, and confirm the agreed result in writing.

commonErrors.error: Arguing with the client about whether the complaint is valid.
commonErrors.prevention: Listen fully, acknowledge the concern, then check the record before you decide on an action.

commonErrors.error: Giving an answer that you have not checked.
commonErrors.prevention: Say you do not yet know, give a time for the answer, and keep that promise.

commonErrors.error: Closing a complaint without follow-up after the fix.
commonErrors.prevention: Set a follow-up date when the complaint is recorded and confirm satisfaction before closing it.

safetyAndRegulatory.point: Client records include names, addresses, contact numbers and photographs of the client's property. Use client information and photographs only for the job, and only with the client's permission.

Refunds, warranties and guarantees for consumer goods and services are governed by the Australian Consumer Law. Do not promise a refund or guarantee beyond what your written terms and your authority allow until a registered adviser confirms the position.

qualityStandard: Every booking is confirmed in writing with included items, excluded items and the client's on-site requirements.
Every complaint has a record showing the date, the client's details, the detail given, the action agreed and the outcome.
Every resolved complaint has a recorded follow-up showing the client's satisfaction, or a note of why satisfaction was not reached.
Escalated matters are passed on in writing to the named person within the same working day.
documentationEvidence: Booking confirmation with scope, exclusions and on-site requirements.
Complaint register entry with date, client details, action, outcome and follow-up date.
Handover note signed or acknowledged by the client, with any open point listed.
summary: Service begins at the first enquiry, and expectations are set in writing before any work starts.
Record what was agreed about the condition of the property or item, and make the handover walk-through a routine.
A complaint is handled in a fixed order: listen, acknowledge, check the record, act within your authority, record, and follow up.

knowledgeChecks.question: A client asks whether a stain will come out. You have not yet seen it. What is the best reply?
options: Yes, it comes out with the standard product on the first visit and there is no need to check it first
Look at it with the client first, say what you can and cannot promise, and confirm the agreement in writing
Say nothing and see what happens during the job and then tell the client what happened afterwards

knowledgeChecks.question: A client complains after handover. What is the first step?
options: Explain why the client is mistaken about the result
Offer a discount straight away, without checking the facts
Listen fully, acknowledge the concern and check the job record

knowledgeChecks.question: Why record a complaint even when it is resolved quickly?
options: Records are only needed for tax purposes and only for the accounts team to review each month
The client must sign it before it counts and the signature must be witnessed by a manager
It shows what happened, what was done and whether the client was satisfied, and helps you spot repeat problems

officialReferences.title: Small business (Office of the Australian Information Commissioner)
officialReferences.covers: Read via summary fetch. The page states most small businesses are not covered by the Privacy Act, with the threshold given as annual turnover of $3 million or less. Exceptions apply regardless of turnover, including health service providers, businesses trading in personal information, credit reporting bodies, related businesses and businesses that have opted in. The page does not name the currency of the threshold. It recommends protecting personal information as good practice. Whether the Act applies to a particular business is not confirmed by this entry and should be checked with the OAIC.

officialReferences.title: Australian Consumer Law: refunds, warranties and guarantees
officialReferences.covers: Read. Supports that consumer guarantees apply to services: a service must be suitable for its purpose, delivered with due care and skill, and supplied within a reasonable time; where a guarantee is not met the business must resolve the problem (repair, replacement, refund or compensation). Not confirmed on this page: that a consumer may reject a service and obtain a refund for a major failure. Publisher: ACCC.
